title: Repaint the Fence
story: A long garden fence has boards painted in different colours over the years. Each colour is a capital letter, so the fence reads like "GGRGBBG".
An artist wants an unbroken one-colour stretch as a mural background. She has paint for only k boards, and can repaint a board any colour. How long a one-colour stretch can she make?
task: Write longestOneColour(boards, k). You may change at most k characters of boards, each to any capital letter. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive equal characters you can make.
constraints: boards contains capital letters A-Z only.

examples.explanation: Repaint the R green: the first four boards become GGGG, using the one repaint. GGRGB would need two repaints (the R and the B). The answer is 4.
Repainting the two B's in RBRBR makes RRRRR, length 5. Every 6-board stretch has three of each colour, so it would need three repaints.

hints: Pick a stretch, like GGRGB. How many repaints make it all one colour, and which colour should you choose?
Keep the stretch's most common colour and repaint the rest. So a stretch works when length - (count of its most common colour) ≤ k.
That rule lets you use a window. Grow it on the right. When it needs more than k repaints, slide the left edge forward one board.

Keep colour counts for the window and the highest count seen so far, top. For each right: count the new board and update top. While windowLength - top > k, remove the left board from the counts and move left. Record the window length. (top never needs to go down: a smaller top can never beat the best length already found.)
bruteForce: Check every stretch: count its colours, and if length - mostCommon ≤ k, record the length.
A 10,000-board fence has about 50 million stretches. Even updating counts as the end moves, that is O(n²) work, mostly on stretches that are obviously too short or too expensive.

walkthrough: A stretch needs length - mostCommon repaints: keep the commonest colour, repaint the others. So slide a window and keep it within budget.
• Add G and G. The window is GG, top is 2, and 0 repaints are needed, so the best length is 2.
• Add R. The window is GGR, top is 2, and 1 repaint is needed, so the best length is 3.
• Add G. The window is GGRG, top is 3, and 1 repaint is needed, so the best length is 4.
• Add B: GGRGB, top 3, repaints 2. Too many. Drop the left G: GRGB, length 4, repaints 4 - 3 = 1 by the rule. Best stays 4.
• Add B: length 5, repaints 2. Drop G: RGBB, length 4. Best stays 4.
• Add G: length 5, repaints 2. Drop R: GBBG, length 4. Best stays 4.
In steps 4 to 6, top stayed 3 even after a G left the window, so the code thinks GRGB needs 1 repaint when it really needs 2. That is safe:
• With a stale top, the window only slides at its current size, a length already proved possible. It never records a longer one.
• The window grows only when a new board pushes top higher. Then top is the real count of that board inside the window, so the longer window really is possible.
solution.timeWhy: Each board enters the window once and leaves at most once; counting is O(1).
solution.takeaway: Turn the rule into a number you can maintain as the window moves (here, length minus the top count). If the window only needs to beat its own best size, it can slide instead of shrinking, and a slightly stale count is safe.
